summary: Describes how the MIT Lincoln Laboratory IBM 360/67 let other ARPANET users log in and use it. After logging in, a user got a whole virtual 360 machine with a virtual console, card reader, printer and disks. The document is a description of one site's service rather than a general standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 109 describes how a network user could connect to Lincoln Laboratory's IBM 360/67. The LOGGER sets up the connection and login, and a SERVER relays console input and output to the CP-67 virtual machine.

subtitle: How Lincoln Laboratory's IBM 360/67 provided network access to its CP-67 system.

tldr.problem: Network users needed a documented way to connect to the Lincoln Laboratory IBM 360/67 and use its CP-67 virtual machine system.
tldr.mechanism: A user establishes connections with the LOGGER using the Initial Connection Protocol, selects ASCII or EBCDIC, and logs in through the LOGGER's account mapping.
tldr.outcome: After login, the user controls a virtual 360 with a console and virtual devices; the RFC describes one host's service rather than a general protocol.

today: RFC 109 describes the login and server service for one Lincoln Laboratory host. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: The Lincoln Laboratory Host
sections.content:
The Lincoln Laboratory IBM 360/67 serves network users by providing access to the CP-67 virtual machine operating system. After login, a user controls a virtual 360 through a virtual 1052 console and can use a virtual card reader, card punch, line printer, and disk devices.

The host's Network Control Program communicates through the IMP using the Host-Host Protocol. The RFC describes this site's service and its operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The host lets a network user log in to a virtual 360. The virtual machine has a console and virtual input, output, and storage devices.

sections.title: Connecting Through the LOGGER
sections.content:
A user starts by making a pair of connections with the LOGGER through the Initial Connection Protocol. The LOGGER listens for a request on socket X'0A 0000 01'. If it accepts another user, it sends a 32-bit receive-socket identifier and closes the initial connection; otherwise, it refuses by closing without completing it.

The user then sends an 8-bit data-type code: X'01' for 7-bit ASCII in 8-bit bytes or X'02' for 8-bit EBCDIC. The LOGGER echoes the code and sends a CP-67 online message. It maps network user IDs and passwords to CP-67 accounts using entries in a LOGGER file.
sections.plainLanguage: The LOGGER first accepts or refuses the connection. If it accepts, the user chooses ASCII or EBCDIC and then follows the usual CP-67 login procedure.

sections.title: Line Input, Prompts, and Interrupts
sections.content:
CP-67 processes input a line at a time. When CP requests a line, the SERVER sends the prompting code X'80'; it buffers received characters until a newline arrives.

A user can send X'80' as an interrupt code to interrupt a running CP process. The user also sends an INS signal on the send link. If the interrupt arrives before buffered input is processed, the SERVER flushes those characters. A separate INS on the receive link can tell the user to retract a prompt when CP has output to send first.
sections.plainLanguage: The server prompts when CP-67 is ready for a line, then collects characters until a newline. A special code can interrupt CP-67, and INS signals coordinate the interruption.

sections.title: ASCII and EBCDIC Conversion
sections.content:
The RFC includes tables for EBCDIC and ASCII graphics and control codes and compares their meanings. It identifies four ASCII codes without EBCDIC counterparts and assigns EBCDIC codes to them.

When converting EBCDIC to ASCII, the RFC specifies that several codes without counterparts become X'FF'. EBCDIC newline is converted to the ASCII carriage-return and line-feed sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: The document provides tables for translating between ASCII and EBCDIC. Some characters without a counterpart are mapped to a substitute code.
